competitor.summary: New York City is home to 3,241 coffee shops, and about a third of those (1,106) are part of larger chains. The biggest players are Dunkin’ with 544 locations, Starbucks with 252, and a handful of smaller chains such as Blank Street Coffee, Gregory’s Coffee, Blue Bottle Coffee, 787 Coffee, Le Cafe Coffee and Matto Espresso, each ranging from 11 to 38 shops. While Hell’s Kitchen is the most crowded market—only 275 weekday subway riders per shop—Elmhurst in Queens is the most under‑served, with 5,096 weekday riders for each coffee shop.

operations.role: Studies what successful cafés do right and what gets cafés in trouble (health grades, closures).
operations.summary: Well‑run cafés tend to earn the top health grade, with 95 % of all NYC coffee shops achieving an A and the highest rates among chains (98 %) and independents (94 %). They avoid the small but serious risk of closure—only 4 % have ever been shut down—by keeping pest‑related issues under control, since two‑thirds of the 119 inspected closures were linked to pests. The most common serious deficiency that can lead to trouble is inadequate cleaning and sanitising of surfaces, a problem that was observed in 1,864 shops.

top_violations.description: Food contact surface not properly washed, rinsed and sanitized after each use and following any activity when contamination may have occurred.
top_violations.tip: Surfaces not cleaned and sanitised properly: sanitise after every use.

top_violations.description: Food not protected from potential source of contamination during storage, preparation, transportation, display or service.
top_violations.tip: Food not protected: cover food, use sneeze guards, label containers.

top_violations.description: Cold TCS food item held above 41 °F; smoked or processed fish held above 38 °F; intact raw eggs held above 45 °F; or reduced oxygen packaged (ROP) TCS foods held above required temperatures except during active necessary preparation.
top_violations.tip: Cold food too warm: keep milk and cold items at 41°F or below; check fridges daily.

top_violations.description: Filth flies or food/refuse/sewage associated with (FRSA) flies or other nuisance pests  in  establishment’s food and/or non-food areas. FRSA flies include house flies, blow flies, bottle flies, flesh flies, drain flies, Phorid flies and fruit flies.
top_violations.tip: Flies: screens, closed bins, clean drains.

top_violations.description: Evidence of mice or live mice in establishment's food or non-food areas.
top_violations.tip: Mice: seal gaps, store food off the floor, use a licensed pest-control service.

top_violations.description: Food Protection Certificate (FPC) not held by manager or supervisor of food operations.
top_violations.tip: No Food Protection Certificate holder on duty: make sure a certified manager is always on shift.

top_violations.description: Wiping cloths not stored clean and dry, or in a sanitizing solution, between uses.
top_violations.tip: Wiping cloths left out: keep them in sanitising solution between uses.

top_violations.description: Hot TCS food item not held at or above 140 °F.
top_violations.tip: Hot food not hot enough: hold hot food at 140°F or above.

lessons.title: Keep an A grade from day one
lessons.text: 95% of coffee shops have an A. Customers see the grade in the window, so a B or C puts you behind most competitors.

lessons.title: Pests are the top reason cafés get shut
lessons.text: 66% of the coffee shops the Health Department closed had a pest problem at that inspection. A pest-control contract and sealing gaps around pipes and doors are must-haves.

lessons.title: Chains run tight processes; independents can too
lessons.text: Chains hold A grades 98% of the time vs 94% for independents. Daily checklists (fridge temperatures, cleaning, pest checks) close that gap.

lessons.title: Don't open where it's already crowded
lessons.text: Areas with few riders per café split the same customers many ways. Look for busy streets that have few cafés (see the map).

picks.name: Downtown Brooklyn-DUMBO-Boerum Hill
picks.why: Downtown Brooklyn‑DUMBO‑Boerum Hill already draws a lot of people—each coffee shop nearby gets about 2,064 weekday subway riders, and the whole area sees over 111,000 subway entries a day, so you’ll have steady foot traffic from commuters and nearby workers who are out from 8 am to 4‑8 pm. With 800 storefronts in the neighborhood and only 43 vacant, there are still a few good spaces left, and the median resident income of roughly $44,300 means locals have decent spending power for a daily cup. All existing cafés have earned an A health‑grade, and the overall market score is 79/100, highlighting strong foot traffic, available locations, and a growing café scene. The main thing to watch is the competition: there are already 53 coffee shops (including 16 chains) and 14 new cafés opened in the past two years, so you’ll need a clear concept or niche to stand out.

trace.content: New study: where should a first-time owner open a coffee shop in NYC? Each of you, report on the whole city first.
Citywide report, please.

New York City is home to 3,241 coffee shops, and about a third of those (1,106) are part of larger chains. The biggest players are Dunkin’ with 544 locations, Starbucks with 252, and a handful of smaller chains such as Blank Street Coffee, Gregory’s Coffee, Blue Bottle Coffee, 787 Coffee, Le Cafe Coffee and Matto Espresso, each ranging from 11 to 38 shops. While Hell’s Kitchen is the most crowded market—only 275 weekday subway riders per shop—Elmhurst in Queens is the most under‑served, with 5,096 weekday riders for each coffee shop.
Citywide report, please.

In the past two years, 780 new coffee shops have opened in New York City, and the overwhelming majority—84%—are independent cafés rather than chain locations. The highest concentration of these openings is in Midtown‑Times Square, where 43 new shops have launched. Among the chains, Dunkin leads with 51 new stores, followed by Starbucks with 16, and smaller entrants such as Cotti Coffee, Matto Espresso, and Luckin Coffee adding between six and seven locations each.
Citywide report, please.

Midtown‑Times Square is the city’s busiest commercial hub, seeing about 413,985 subway entries on an average weekday. It also has the most empty storefronts of any area, with 181 of its 2,744 spaces currently vacant. This combination of high foot traffic and available units makes Midtown‑Times Square a promising spot to consider for your new coffee shop.
Citywide report, please.

Well‑run cafés tend to earn the top health grade, with 95 % of all NYC coffee shops achieving an A and the highest rates among chains (98 %) and independents (94 %). They avoid the small but serious risk of closure—only 4 % have ever been shut down—by keeping pest‑related issues under control, since two‑thirds of the 119 inspected closures were linked to pests. The most common serious deficiency that can lead to trouble is inadequate cleaning and sanitising of surfaces, a problem that was observed in 1,864 shops.
